solution.concept_anchor: EoDB Index publishing institution
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because WEF publishes the widely cited Global Competitiveness Index, which is frequently confused with the Doing Business Index in newspaper coverage.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): WEF publishes the Global Competitiveness Index, not the Doing Business Report.
Eliminate (c): IMF publishes the World Economic Outlook and Article IV consultations — no business-environment ranking.
Eliminate (d): UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report focused on FDI flows, not regulatory ease rankings.
Confirm (b): The Doing Business Report was a flagship publication of the World Bank Group — correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: A partially prepared student often attributes the EoDB Index to the WEF because the WEF's Global Competitiveness Index also ranks countries on economic metrics and receives comparable media coverage around the same time each year. The trap is compounded because some news articles loosely refer to 'World Bank' and 'IMF' interchangeably as 'multilateral institutions.' A student who has not pinned down which institution publishes which index will almost certainly select (a) or (c) under time pressure.
solution.final_explanation:
The Doing Business Report was a flagship publication of the World Bank Group, distinct from reports by other multilateral institutions.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: WEF publishes the Global Competitiveness Index (GCI), which covers broader pillars like innovation, infrastructure, and institutions — not just regulatory ease.
• Option (b) — Correct: The World Bank Group published the annual Doing Business Report until it was discontinued in September 2021.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The IMF publishes the World Economic Outlook, Global Financial Stability Report, and Fiscal Monitor — none focused on business regulatory ease rankings.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: UNCTAD's flagship publication is the World Investment Report, which tracks FDI flows and investment policy trends.

Value Addition:
• The World Bank also publishes the World Development Report (WDR) and World Development Indicators (WDI) — distinct from the Doing Business Report.
• The successor to the Doing Business Index is the Business Ready (B-READY) Index, launched in 2024.
• The EoDB index covered 190 economies before its discontinuation.

solution.concept_anchor: EoDB discontinuation and data manipulation scandal

statement_analysis.statement: The World Bank halted the Doing Business Report in 2021 citing data irregularities identified in the 2018 and 2020 editions.
statement_analysis.reason: The World Bank officially suspended the report in September 2021 after an independent investigation found data manipulation in the 2018 and 2020 editions.

statement_analysis.statement: Among the countries alleged to have benefited from manipulated rankings were China, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Brazil.
statement_analysis.reason: Brazil was not among the countries implicated; the countries alleged to have benefited were China, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Azerbaijan.

statement_analysis.statement: Christine Lagarde, in her capacity as IMF Managing Director, was among senior officials whose conduct was scrutinised in connection with the data irregularities.
statement_analysis.reason: The controversy implicated Christine Lagarde (then IMF Managing Director, previously World Bank-connected through the investigation timeline) and World Bank President David Malpass among others.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who recall 'Brazil' from BRICS discussions may substitute it for 'Azerbaijan,' which is a far less prominent name in standard coaching material.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: World Bank halted the report in September 2021 citing 2018 and 2020 editions — this is correct.
Check Statement 2: The countries named are China, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Azerbaijan — Brazil was NOT implicated, making Statement 2 incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Christine Lagarde's conduct was among those scrutinized — correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 replaces 'Azerbaijan' with 'Brazil.' A student who recalls the broad contours of the scandal — that BRICS-adjacent and Gulf countries were involved — may accept Brazil without scrutiny, especially under time pressure. Azerbaijan's inclusion is a specific and less-recalled detail that separates precise preparation from superficial familiarity.
solution.final_explanation:
The World Bank's Doing Business Report was discontinued in September 2021 following an independent investigation that found data irregularities in the 2018 and 2020 editions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The World Bank explicitly cited the 2018 and 2020 editions as the ones affected by irregular adjustments.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The countries alleged to have benefited were China, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Azerbaijan — not Brazil. Substituting Brazil for Azerbaijan is the deliberate trap here.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Christine Lagarde and then-World Bank President David Malpass were among the senior officials whose roles in the data process were scrutinized by independent investigators.

Value Addition:
• The scandal raised broader questions about index-based policymaking — whether sovereign rankings incentivize data manipulation by powerful member-states.
• David Malpass later resigned as World Bank President in 2023 amid separate controversies.
• The controversy reinforced calls for greater transparency in the methodology of multilateral indices.

solution.concept_anchor: B-READY Index pillars and methodology

statement_analysis.statement: The Business Ready (B-READY) Index, launched in 2024, evaluates countries on four pillars: Regulatory Framework, Public Services, Operational Efficiency, and Innovation Climate.
statement_analysis.reason: B-READY covers exactly three pillars — Regulatory Framework, Public Services, and Operational Efficiency. 'Innovation Climate' is not a B-READY pillar.

statement_analysis.statement: A key distinction of B-READY from its predecessor is that it incorporates the quality of regulation, not merely the speed or ease of compliance, thereby addressing the 'race to the bottom' criticism of the earlier index.
statement_analysis.reason: B-READY explicitly incorporates regulatory quality so that countries cannot improve rankings simply by deregulating recklessly — a direct response to the EoDB critique.

statement_analysis.statement: B-READY evaluates ten topic areas aligned with the business lifecycle, consistent with the number of parameters used in the discontinued Doing Business Index.
statement_analysis.reason: Both the EoDB and B-READY use 10 topic areas/parameters, though the specific topics and their definitions differ.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know B-READY has 'multiple pillars' may accept four pillars as plausible, especially since 'Innovation Climate' sounds like a legitimate World Bank category.
elimination_logic: Examine Statement 1: B-READY has three pillars — Regulatory Framework, Public Services, Operational Efficiency. Adding 'Innovation Climate' as a fourth pillar is fabricated — Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Examine Statement 2: The quality-of-regulation distinction is the defining feature of B-READY — this is correct, so Statement 2 is NOT among incorrect ones.
Examine Statement 3: Both indices use 10 topic areas — correct, so Statement 3 is also NOT incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is incorrect — select option (b): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap adds a plausible-sounding fourth pillar ('Innovation Climate') to B-READY's actual three pillars. Students who have only a broad recollection of B-READY being 'more comprehensive than EoDB' may accept four pillars as reasonable. The key fact is three pillars exactly: Regulatory Framework, Public Services, and Operational Efficiency.
solution.final_explanation:
The Business Ready (B-READY) Index was launched by the World Bank in 2024 as the successor to the discontinued Doing Business Index.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: B-READY is structured around exactly three pillars — Regulatory Framework, Public Services, and Operational Efficiency. 'Innovation Climate' is not a B-READY pillar; its addition here is a deliberate distortion.
• Statement 2 — Correct: B-READY incorporates regulatory quality assessment, ensuring countries cannot game rankings through deregulation alone — directly addressing the 'race to the bottom' criticism of EoDB.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Like the EoDB, B-READY also evaluates 10 topic areas, though their definitions are updated to reflect current business realities.

Value Addition:
• The EoDB was criticized for incentivizing deregulation rather than good regulation — B-READY attempts to correct this by rewarding quality alongside speed.
• B-READY covers all stages of the business lifecycle — from entry to operations to exit.
• The World Bank conducted pilot assessments in select economies before the full 2024 launch of B-READY.

solution.concept_anchor: EoDB methodology — DTF score and equal weighting

statement_analysis.statement: The Doing Business Index assigned equal weight to each of its 10 parameters in computing the overall ranking.
statement_analysis.reason: All 10 parameters were equally weighted — no single parameter like 'Enforcing Contracts' or 'Getting Credit' had a higher or lower weight in the final score.

statement_analysis.statement: The Distance to Frontier (DTF) score measured a country's performance relative to the best-performing country in each indicator, allowing absolute progress to be tracked over time.
statement_analysis.reason: DTF was designed precisely to measure absolute performance against a defined best practice frontier, enabling year-on-year comparison even when the frontier itself changes.

statement_analysis.statement: The survey methodology underlying the EoDB used actual transaction data submitted by businesses operating in the surveyed economies.
statement_analysis.reason: The EoDB used a standardized 'case study' firm methodology — responses came from legal and regulatory experts, not actual business transaction records.

statement_analysis.statement: The 10 parameters of the EoDB included Dealing with Construction Permits, Getting Electricity, and Resolving Insolvency among others.
statement_analysis.reason: These three are explicitly among the 10 officially recognized parameters of the Doing Business Index.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 3 as wrong may still doubt Statement 2, confusing DTF's absolute-measurement purpose with a relative ranking mechanism.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — equal weighting across all 10 parameters is a key methodological feature.
Statement 2 is correct — DTF measures absolute distance from a defined best-practice frontier.
Statement 3 is incorrect — EoDB used standardized case-study firms and expert responses, not actual business transaction data.
Statement 4 is correct — Construction Permits, Electricity, and Insolvency are all standard EoDB parameters.
Three of four statements are correct — select option (c): Only three.
solution.final_explanation:
The EoDB Index methodology had several distinctive features that UPSC tests frequently.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Equal weighting across 10 parameters | Correct |
| DTF measures absolute performance | Correct |
| Based on actual business transaction data | Incorrect |
| Includes Construction Permits, Electricity, Insolvency | Correct |

• Statements 1, 2, 4 — Correct: Equal weighting, DTF as absolute measure, and the named parameters are all accurate features of EoDB methodology.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The EoDB used a hypothetical standardized firm ('case study') approach — lawyers, accountants, and regulatory experts answered questions about a notional scenario, not real businesses.

Value Addition:
• DTF allowed comparison across years even if country composition changed — a methodological advantage over pure rank-based systems.
• The case-study approach was also a criticism: it captured de jure regulations, not on-the-ground implementation realities.
• B-READY attempts to address this by also measuring public service delivery quality, not just regulatory text.

Parameters Where India Performed Best vs Worst

solution.concept_anchor: India's EoDB parameter-wise rank in DB2020
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it correctly matches Getting Credit and Protecting Minority Investors but swaps the ranks for Enforcing Contracts and Resolving Insolvency, which many students recall only vaguely.
elimination_logic: Protecting Minority Investors: India ranked 13 in DB2020 — confirm List I item A matches List II item 2.
Getting Credit: India ranked 25 in DB2020 — confirm List I item B matches List II item 4.
Resolving Insolvency: improved to rank 52 after IBC 2016 — confirm List I item C matches List II item 3.
Enforcing Contracts: India's worst parameter at rank 163 — confirm List I item D matches List II item 1. This gives A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1 — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the fact that students recall India's contrasting performance — very good on some parameters, very poor on others — but mix up the exact ranks. 'Enforcing Contracts' (rank 163) and 'Resolving Insolvency' (rank 52) are often swapped because both relate to legal dispute resolution. Similarly, 'Getting Credit' (25) and 'Protecting Minority Investors' (13) are adjacent in students' memory as 'India's good parameters.'
solution.final_explanation:
India's DB2020 parameter-wise rankings revealed sharp contrasts between its strongest and weakest areas.

Correct matching: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1.

• Protecting Minority Investors (A) → Rank 13: India's best-performing parameter in DB2020, bolstered by Companies Act 2013 amendments on related-party transactions and SEBI disclosure norms.
• Getting Credit (B) → Rank 25: India's second-best parameter, improved through SARFAESI amendments, CERSAI registry, and expanded credit bureau coverage.
• Resolving Insolvency (C) → Rank 52: A dramatic improvement from rank 136 in 2017, driven directly by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 and the NCLT infrastructure.
• Enforcing Contracts (D) → Rank 163: India's worst-performing parameter, reflecting average contract enforcement times of ~1,445 days against a global average of ~589 days.

Value Addition:
• The Commercial Courts Act 2015 was introduced to address Enforcing Contracts — its impact on rank was limited during the EoDB era.
• Starting a Business also remained a challenge despite SPICe+ reforms on MCA portal.
• India's overall rank improved from 142 (2014) to 63 (2020) — a jump of 79 positions in six years.

solution.concept_anchor: India's EoDB survey cities — Mumbai and Delhi only
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are individually correct, tempting students to assume R explains A without checking whether the causal connection holds.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? India's EoDB rank was surveyed using only Mumbai and Delhi, not all major metros — this is factually correct.
Step 2 — Is R correct? India did improve from rank 142 in 2014 to rank 63 in 2020, a jump of 79 positions — this is factually correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? The overall rank improvement does not explain or cause the limitation of survey cities to Mumbai and Delhi — that is a methodological design choice by the World Bank, independent of India's rank trajectory.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question exploits the tendency of students to accept option (a) when both A and R are individually true. The causal trap is subtle: India's rank improvement is a real and significant fact, but it has no explanatory relationship to the methodological decision to survey only two cities. The two-city limitation was a World Bank methodology norm applied to all large countries — it did not change based on a country's reform performance.
solution.final_explanation:
This assertion-reason tests the distinction between correlation of facts and causal explanation.

Assertion (A): For the purpose of the Doing Business Index, only Mumbai and Delhi were surveyed to represent India — this is correct. The World Bank's methodology for large economies was to survey the two largest business cities, and for India these were Mumbai and Delhi (not Bengaluru, Chennai, or Kolkata).

Reason (R): India improved its overall EoDB rank by 79 positions between 2014 and 2020 — this is also correct. India moved from rank 142 to rank 63 in this period and was among the top 10 improvers for three consecutive years.

Causal Link: R does not explain A. The two-city survey design is a World Bank methodology standard applied across large economies — it is entirely independent of whether India's rank improved or stagnated. A country's rank trajectory has no bearing on how many cities the World Bank chooses to survey.

Value Addition:
• The two-city limitation was a key criticism — Delhi and Mumbai do not represent India's diverse regulatory environments (e.g., startup hubs like Bengaluru, manufacturing zones like Pune).
• B-READY is expected to cover more cities/locations per country.
• India was among the top 10 improvers in the Doing Business Report for 2016, 2017, and 2018 consecutively.

solution.concept_anchor: IBC 2016 and Resolving Insolvency rank improvement timeline
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because it correctly places IBC enactment before the rank improvement but reverses the order of NCLT establishment and the DB2020 report, which students rarely recall in sequence.
elimination_logic: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code was enacted in 2016 — this must come first among the four events.
NCLT was established in 2016 as part of IBC implementation — immediately follows IBC enactment.
India's Resolving Insolvency rank jumped to 52 — this was recorded in DB2020, published in October 2019.

India's previous Resolving Insolvency rank of 136 was in DB2017 — this precedes the jump, so the correct order is: IBC enacted → NCLT established → rank at 136 (DB2017) → rank improved to 52 (DB2020).
Correct sequence: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap is that students may confuse when the rank of 136 was recorded (DB2017, i.e., data for 2016) versus when the improvement to 52 appeared (DB2020). Both fall within a 3-year window, making sequencing genuinely difficult without precise year-pinning.
solution.final_explanation:
The IBC reform and its impact on the EoDB's Resolving Insolvency parameter unfolded in a clear sequence.

Correct order: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4

1. IBC enacted (2016): The foundational legislation that created a time-bound insolvency resolution framework.
2. NCLT established (2016): The National Company Law Tribunal was the institutional infrastructure created to adjudicate insolvency cases under IBC.
3. Resolving Insolvency rank at 136 (DB2017): India's rank in this parameter in the first Doing Business Report after IBC was enacted — reforms had not yet shown measurable impact.
4. Resolving Insolvency rank jumps to 52 (DB2020): By DB2020, India's rank had improved dramatically, reflecting reduced resolution time and improved recovery rates.

Why other options fail: Options placing DB2020 before DB2017, or NCLT before IBC, are chronologically impossible — IBC is the enabling legislation for NCLT's insolvency jurisdiction.

Value Addition:
• IBC reduced average resolution time from ~4.3 years to under 2 years (target: 180 days for regular cases, 270 days for complex ones).
• Recovery rate improved from ~26 cents to ~71 cents on the dollar under IBC.
• NCLAT (National Company Law Appellate Tribunal) serves as the appellate body over NCLT decisions.

solution.concept_anchor: EoDB Enforcing Contracts — court-based measurement only
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know arbitration reforms are meant to improve dispute resolution speed may assume they directly improve the EoDB Enforcing Contracts rank, without knowing the parameter measures only court-based enforcement.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a reform targeting out-of-court arbitration resolution — identify which EoDB parameter this reform aims to address.

Eliminate (a): Arbitration reforms may reduce litigation burden, but the EoDB Enforcing Contracts parameter specifically measures time and cost in the formal court system — arbitration outcomes are NOT captured.
Eliminate (b): Trading Across Borders relates to customs, ports, and trade logistics — entirely unrelated to dispute resolution reforms.
Eliminate (d): Paying Taxes relates to tax filing, payments, and compliance — no connection to contract dispute resolution.
Confirm (c): The intended target is Enforcing Contracts — but the limitation is that the EoDB surveys only court-based proceedings, so arbitration reforms do not improve the rank.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: A superficially prepared student will select (a), reasoning that 'arbitration reforms improve dispute resolution, which improves the Enforcing Contracts parameter.' The trap is that the EoDB's Enforcing Contracts parameter exclusively measured court-based commercial litigation time and cost. Out-of-court mechanisms like arbitration were outside the survey's scope. This is an explicitly annotated UPSC trap in the key dimensions.
solution.final_explanation:
India amended the Arbitration and Conciliation Act multiple times (2015, 2019, 2021) to reduce arbitration timelines and make India an arbitration-friendly jurisdiction.

The parameter this reform targets is Enforcing Contracts — but the critical limitation is that the EoDB measured Enforcing Contracts exclusively through formal court proceedings. The survey asked: how long does it take to resolve a standardized commercial dispute through the courts? Arbitration settlements, however fast, were outside this measurement scope.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Arbitration reforms cannot directly improve the Enforcing Contracts rank under EoDB methodology because the parameter measures court-based enforcement only.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Trading Across Borders measures time, cost, and documentation for imports and exports — unrelated to commercial dispute resolution.
• Option (c) — Correct: Enforcing Contracts is the intended parameter, but the reforms face a methodological blind spot in EoDB's court-centric measurement.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Paying Taxes measures the number of tax payments, time to comply, and total tax rate — no connection to contract disputes.

Value Addition:
• India ranked 163/190 in Enforcing Contracts in DB2020 — its worst parameter.
• Average contract enforcement time in India: ~1,445 days vs. global average ~589 days.
• The Commercial Courts Act 2015 was specifically designed to address this but had limited measurable impact on the rank.

solution.concept_anchor: Distinguishing EoDB from broader competitiveness indices
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because Heritage Foundation's Index of Economic Freedom sounds like it could measure regulatory ease for businesses, which students may conflate with the EoDB's focus.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: which indices focus specifically on regulatory processes for small domestic firms or business ease — the EoDB's specific domain.
WEF Global Competitiveness Index covers innovation, institutions, and infrastructure — broader than regulatory ease alone; does NOT belong to narrow 'regulatory ease for small firms' category.
UNCTAD World Investment Report focuses on FDI flows and investment policy — not regulatory ease for domestic SMEs.
Heritage Foundation Index of Economic Freedom covers rule of law, government size, regulatory efficiency, and open markets — broader dimensions.

The Doing Business Index is the only one that narrowly measured regulatory processes for a small-medium domestic firm — WEF GCI (b) is the odd one out among indices that are NOT EoDB-type narrow regulatory indices.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The question asks which index does NOT share the characteristic of being a broad multi-dimensional economic competitiveness index — i.e., which is the narrow regulatory-ease-only index. The odd one out is the EoDB itself (represented here as the Doing Business Index) in a group of broader indices, but framed differently: which among the listed indices measures the BROADEST set of factors, making it unlike the EoDB's narrow firm-level regulatory focus? WEF GCI covers 12 pillars including innovation and institutions — broadest of all.
solution.final_explanation:
The question tests the ability to distinguish the EoDB's narrow regulatory focus from the broader, multi-dimensional indices.

• Option (a) — UNCTAD World Investment Report: Focuses on FDI flows and investment policy — does not measure domestic business regulatory ease; a different dimension entirely.
• Option (b) — WEF Global Competitiveness Index: Covers 12 pillars including innovation, institutions, infrastructure, macroeconomic stability, health, and education — the broadest of the listed indices. Unlike the others, it measures national competitiveness comprehensively, not just business regulation. This is the odd one out among indices that the others share with EoDB in terms of economic policy focus.
• Option (c) — Heritage Foundation Index of Economic Freedom: Covers rule of law, government size, regulatory efficiency, and open markets — while broader than EoDB, it includes regulatory dimensions.
• Option (d) — World Bank Doing Business Index: The narrow, firm-level regulatory process index — the reference point.

Value Addition:
• WEF GCI was restructured in 2018 to better capture the Fourth Industrial Revolution — innovation and ICT adoption became more prominent.
• The Heritage Index scores countries from 0 to 100 on economic freedom.
• None of the other indices use a 'case study firm' methodology like EoDB did.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The introduction of GST in 2017 subsumed 17 central and state taxes, directly reducing the number of tax payments for businesses and significantly improving India's rank in the Paying Taxes parameter of the EoDB to among the top 50 globally.
statement_analysis.reason: While GST did subsume multiple taxes and reduce tax payments, India's rank in Paying Taxes remained moderate — approximately rank 115 in DB2020 — far from the top 50.

statement_analysis.reason: The EoDB Paying Taxes parameter also measures compliance hours — the multiple GST return requirements initially increased this burden, partially offsetting gains from reduced tax payment count.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who associate GST with improved tax ease may accept Statement 1 as fully correct without checking whether India actually reached the top 50 in Paying Taxes.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: GST did reduce the number of taxes — correct so far. But India's Paying Taxes rank in DB2020 was approximately 115, not in the top 50 — the 'top 50' claim makes Statement 1 incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Multiple return filings (GSTR-1, 3B, annual) did initially increase compliance hours — this is a documented trade-off and Statement 2 is correct.

solution.final_explanation:

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: GST subsumed 17 central and state taxes (correct premise), but India's Paying Taxes rank in DB2020 was approximately 115 — well outside the top 50. The rank did improve, but not to top-50 levels. The addition of 'top 50 globally' renders the statement false.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Paying Taxes parameter measures not just the number of tax payments but also total tax rate and time/hours spent on compliance. The initial GST regime required businesses to file GSTR-1 (outward supplies), GSTR-3B (summary return), and an annual return — multiple filings that paradoxically increased compliance hours despite structural simplification.

Value Addition:
• The EoDB Paying Taxes parameter covers three sub-components: number of payments, time to comply (hours/year), and total tax and contribution rate.
• GST Council rationalization over the years has progressively simplified filing requirements — QRMP scheme reduced return frequency for smaller taxpayers.
• Pre-filled GST returns and e-invoicing are ongoing reforms to reduce compliance burden.

statement_analysis.statement: India's rank of 25 in the Getting Credit parameter of DB2020 was primarily attributable to reforms in secured transactions law, including amendments to the SARFAESI Act and the creation of the CERSAI registry.
statement_analysis.reason: SARFAESI amendments enabling faster asset recovery and CERSAI (Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest) for collateral tracking directly improved the 'Strength of Legal Rights Index' sub-component of Getting Credit.

statement_analysis.statement: The Getting Credit parameter in the EoDB comprised two sub-indices: the Strength of Legal Rights Index and the Depth of Credit Information Index.
statement_analysis.reason: These two sub-indices are the official components of the Getting Credit parameter — one measuring legal frameworks for secured lending, the other measuring credit bureau coverage and data depth.

statement_analysis.statement: CIBIL (Credit Information Bureau India Limited) is India's only credit information company, and its expansion directly improved the Depth of Credit Information Index under the Getting Credit parameter.
statement_analysis.reason: India has four credit information companies — CIBIL, Equifax, Experian, and CRIF High Mark — not just CIBIL alone. The claim of CIBIL being 'India's only' credit bureau is false.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who associate credit bureaus with 'CIBIL' (as the dominant and most well-known bureau) may not recall that there are three other RBI-licensed credit information companies.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — SARFAESI amendments and CERSAI registry are documented contributors to India's Getting Credit rank improvement.
Statement 2 is correct — Strength of Legal Rights Index and Depth of Credit Information Index are the two official sub-components.
Statement 3 is incorrect — India has four credit information companies (CIBIL, Equifax, Experian, CRIF High Mark), not one.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the designed trap: CIBIL dominates public discourse about credit scores, making 'India's only credit bureau' a plausible-sounding claim. Students who equate CIBIL with the entire credit information ecosystem will accept Statement 3 as correct, leading them to select option (d) instead of (b).
solution.final_explanation:
India's strong performance in Getting Credit (rank 25 in DB2020) reflects two distinct reform tracks.

• Statement 1 — Correct: SARFAESI Act amendments enabled lenders to recover secured assets without court intervention, and CERSAI created a centralized registry for security interests — both improving the legal rights framework for creditors.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Getting Credit has exactly two sub-indices: (i) Strength of Legal Rights Index — measuring secured transactions and collateral laws, and (ii) Depth of Credit Information Index — measuring credit bureau coverage, data quality, and borrower information availability.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: India has four RBI-licensed credit information companies — CIBIL (TransUnion), Equifax, Experian India, and CRIF High Mark. CIBIL's brand dominance in public awareness does not make it the 'only' credit bureau.

Value Addition:
• CERSAI was established under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act — it prevents fraud by ensuring the same asset is not pledged as collateral multiple times.
• Getting Credit rank 25 was India's second-best parameter in DB2020 after Protecting Minority Investors (rank 13).
• RBI mandates banks to report all credit exposures above a threshold to credit bureaus — this directly boosts the Depth of Credit Information sub-score.

solution.concept_anchor: EoDB methodological limitations and coverage gaps

statement_analysis.statement: The Doing Business Index measured both the formal legal framework for business regulations and actual implementation on the ground, giving a complete picture of the business environment.
statement_analysis.reason: EoDB measured only 'de jure' regulations — what the law says — not 'de facto' implementation. Ground-level corruption, inspector discretion, and actual delays were not captured.

statement_analysis.statement: The EoDB survey focused exclusively on small-to-medium domestic firms, thereby excluding FDI-specific barriers, large infrastructure project approvals, and labor market flexibility from its measurement scope.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an accurate description of the EoDB's stated limitations — it was explicitly designed for a standardized SME scenario and did not capture barriers relevant to large foreign investors or infrastructure developers.

statement_analysis.statement: The Doing Business Index incorporated assessments of corruption levels, environmental compliance costs, and labor market flexibility as part of its composite score.
statement_analysis.reason: None of these three dimensions — corruption, environmental regulations, or labor market flexibility — were included in the EoDB composite score. These were among the most cited omissions.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know EoDB had limitations may accept Statement 2 as also being an 'incorrect' statement, confusing a limitation (which is a real feature) with an error.
elimination_logic: Examine Statement 1: EoDB measured de jure regulations only, NOT actual implementation — 'complete picture' is false. Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Examine Statement 2: EoDB did focus on SMEs and explicitly excluded FDI barriers, large projects, and labor flexibility — this statement accurately describes the limitation, so it IS correct, not incorrect.
Examine Statement 3: Corruption, environmental costs, and labor flexibility were NOT measured by EoDB — 'incorporated' is false. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 accurately describes a real limitation of EoDB — that it covered only SMEs and excluded FDI barriers and labor flexibility. A student may mistake this statement as 'incorrect' because it sounds critical of EoDB, but it is factually accurate. The question asks which statements are NOT correct, so Statement 2 must be excluded from the answer.
solution.final_explanation:
The EoDB Index had well-documented methodological limitations that distinguished it from a comprehensive business environment assessment.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (NOT correct): EoDB measured only 'de jure' regulatory frameworks — the text of laws and procedures. It did not assess whether these laws were implemented faithfully, making it blind to corruption, informal payments, or bureaucratic delays.
• Statement 2 — Correct: This accurately describes the EoDB's known limitation. It assessed a hypothetical standardized SME and thus could not capture FDI-related barriers (like sectoral caps or approval timelines for foreign investors) or infrastructure project bottlenecks.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (NOT correct): Corruption, environmental regulations, and labor market flexibility were explicitly NOT part of the EoDB composite score — these are among the most frequently cited gaps in the index's coverage.

Value Addition:
• The 'de jure vs. de facto' gap is a foundational critique: India could reform laws on paper without changing ground-level implementation, yet see rank improvement.
• Labor regulation was once part of EoDB (as 'Employing Workers') but was removed from the ranking calculation in 2009 after controversy.
• B-READY attempts to partially address these gaps by assessing actual public service delivery, not just regulatory text.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are individually accurate, and students may instinctively link 'labor reform' with 'EoDB improvement' without knowing that the Employing Workers parameter was removed from ranking calculation in 2009.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? India's 4 Labour Codes consolidating 44 central laws are not captured in EoDB ranking — correct, because EoDB had no dedicated labor regulation parameter in its ranking calculation.

statement_analysis.reason: The Jan Vishwas Act 2023 amended 183 provisions across 42 central Acts, replacing imprisonment for minor offences with monetary penalties — decriminalization of procedural violations.

statement_analysis.statement: Decriminalization of minor offences under the Jan Vishwas Act is equivalent to deregulation — both remove legal consequences for the specified acts.
statement_analysis.reason: Decriminalization is not the same as deregulation. Decriminalization removes criminal liability (imprisonment) but retains civil penalties (fines). Deregulation removes the regulatory requirement entirely. Under Jan Vishwas, violations still attract fines — only the criminal prosecution pathway is removed.

statement_analysis.statement: The reforms under the Jan Vishwas Act are primarily relevant to the 'Starting a Business' and 'Dealing with Construction Permits' parameters within the EoDB framework, as they reduce the fear of criminal prosecution during the business entry phase.
statement_analysis.reason: These two parameters involve the most procedural steps where minor non-compliance could previously trigger criminal liability — Jan Vishwas reforms directly address this chilling effect on business entry.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who accept the 'decriminalization = deregulation' conflation will treat Statement 2 as correct and select all three as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Jan Vishwas amended 183 provisions across 42 Acts, converting imprisonment to fines — correct.
Statement 2: Decriminalization ≠ deregulation. Decriminalization removes criminal liability but retains civil penalties (fines). Deregulation removes the rule entirely. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Jan Vishwas targets Starting a Business and Construction Permits pain points — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the common conflation of 'decriminalization' and 'deregulation' — two legally distinct concepts. A student who hears 'decriminalization' and thinks 'the activity is now allowed freely' will accept Statement 2 as correct. The precise distinction — criminal liability is removed but civil penalty (fine) remains — is the examiner's intended test point.
solution.final_explanation:
The Jan Vishwas Act 2023 introduced a critical EoDB reform by addressing the 'fear of prosecution' barrier to business entry.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2023 decriminalized 183 provisions spread across 42 Acts, converting prison terms for minor procedural lapses into monetary fines.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Decriminalization and deregulation are legally distinct. Decriminalization removes only criminal prosecution — the underlying obligation and civil fine remain. Deregulation eliminates the regulatory requirement altogether. Under Jan Vishwas, businesses must still comply; they just face fines, not imprisonment, for minor lapses.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Starting a Business and Dealing with Construction Permits are the EoDB parameters most affected by the fear of prosecution for minor procedural violations — Jan Vishwas reforms reduce this deterrent.

Value Addition:
• Companies Act amendments separately removed imprisonment for minor procedural violations like late filing of annual returns.
• Jan Vishwas 2.0 (proposed) aims to extend decriminalization further across more Acts.

solution.final_explanation:
The sequence from Doing Business Report to its discontinuation and eventual replacement followed a clear causal chain.

solution.concept_anchor: IBC impact metrics — time, recovery rate, NCLT linkage

statement_analysis.statement: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 reduced the average time for insolvency resolution from approximately 4.3 years to under 2 years.
statement_analysis.reason: Pre-IBC, average resolution time under the old SICA/winding-up regime was approximately 4.3 years. IBC's 180/270-day timeline brought this significantly below 2 years on average.

statement_analysis.statement: Under IBC, the recovery rate for creditors improved from approximately 26 cents to approximately 71 cents on the dollar.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the documented improvement cited in the Doing Business Report and World Bank assessments — recovery rates improved from ~26 cents pre-IBC to ~71 cents post-IBC.

statement_analysis.statement: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) adjudicates insolvency cases under IBC, while the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) handles all appeals against NCLT orders.
statement_analysis.reason: Appeals against NCLT orders under IBC go to NCLAT (National Company Law Appellate Tribunal), not DRT. DRTs handle bank loan recovery under SARFAESI and DRT Act — a separate mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: India's rank in 'Resolving Insolvency' in the Doing Business Index improved from 136 in DB2017 to 52 in DB2020 following IBC reforms.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precisely documented rank improvement in the Resolving Insolvency parameter — from rank 136 to rank 52 between DB2017 and DB2020.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who recall 'IBC improved everything related to insolvency' may accept Statement 3 without knowing the specific appellate architecture distinguishing NCLAT from DRT.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — 4.3 years to under 2 years is the documented IBC impact on resolution time.
Statement 2 is correct — 26 cents to 71 cents recovery rate improvement is documented in World Bank data.
Statement 3 is incorrect — NCLAT, not DRT, handles appeals against NCLT orders. DRTs operate under a separate legal framework.
Statement 4 is correct — rank 136 (DB2017) to rank 52 (DB2020) is the precise documented improvement.
Three of four are correct — select option (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 conflates two distinct dispute resolution tribunals — NCLAT and DRT — by attributing NCLAT's appellate function to DRT. DRTs are associated with bank loan recovery and SARFAESI enforcement, and students who know 'NCLT → insolvency, DRT → bank loans' may still incorrectly assign appellate function to DRT under IBC. The correct appellate body is NCLAT.
solution.final_explanation:
IBC 2016 produced measurable, benchmarkable improvements across multiple dimensions of insolvency resolution.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Resolution time reduced from 4.3 years to under 2 years | Correct |
| Recovery rate improved from ~26 to ~71 cents on dollar | Correct |
| DRT handles appeals against NCLT under IBC | Incorrect |
| Rank improved from 136 (DB2017) to 52 (DB2020) | Correct |

• Statements 1, 2, 4 — Correct: These are the three key quantitative outcomes of IBC reforms that directly drove the Resolving Insolvency rank improvement.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: NCLAT (National Company Law Appellate Tribunal) handles appeals against NCLT orders under IBC. DRTs (Debt Recovery Tribunals) operate under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act 1993 and SARFAESI Act — an entirely separate recovery mechanism.

Value Addition:
• IBC has a hierarchy: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) → Appellate Authority (NCLAT) → Supreme Court.
• The 180-day resolution timeline under IBC can be extended by 90 days in complex cases — total 270 days.
• Pre-IBC, India had multiple overlapping insolvency regimes: SICA, RDDBFI Act, Companies Act winding-up — IBC consolidated these.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because WEF GCI is the most widely cited competitiveness index and students may assume the scenario's description of 'comprehensive competitiveness' fits GCI — but the scenario specifies regulatory ease for domestic SMEs, which is EoDB's unique scope.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes an index measuring only regulatory processes for a standardized domestic SME — narrow, firm-level, regulatory scope.
Eliminate (a): WEF GCI covers 12 broad pillars including innovation, institutions, infrastructure, and market size — not a narrow SME regulatory process index.
Eliminate (c): UNCTAD WIR focuses on global FDI flows and multinational investment patterns — not domestic SME regulation.
Eliminate (d): Heritage Foundation Index covers rule of law, government size, fiscal health, and trade freedom — broader dimensions than firm-level regulatory procedures.
Confirm (b): The World Bank's Doing Business Index is the only index that specifically measured regulatory procedures for a standardized small domestic firm — matching the scenario precisely.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario is designed to test whether students can identify the EoDB's unique narrow focus: a standardized domestic SME going through regulated business procedures. WEF GCI is the key conflation trap — many students use 'competitiveness' and 'ease of doing business' interchangeably, not realizing GCI is far broader (12 pillars, includes innovation, macroeconomics, health, education) while EoDB was narrowly procedural.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario describes an index with a very specific and narrow scope: regulatory procedures for a standardized small domestic firm, measured through a case-study methodology with a 190-economy coverage.

This is the World Bank's Doing Business Index.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: WEF Global Competitiveness Index measures 12 pillars — enabling environment, human capital, markets, innovation ecosystem. It includes factors like R&D expenditure, ICT adoption, and infrastructure quality — far broader than SME regulatory procedures.

• Option (d) — Incorrect: Heritage Foundation's Index of Economic Freedom measures fiscal freedom, government integrity, rule of law, and trade freedom — broader governance and macroeconomic dimensions.

• The EoDB's case-study firm was typically assumed to be 100% domestically owned, with specific employee and revenue thresholds.

• The Heritage Index scores countries from 0 (least free) to 100 (most free) on 12 components.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because 'Shareholder Suits Index' sounds like it could be a litigation-related concept rather than a shareholder protection sub-index, leading students to question whether it belongs.

solution.concept_anchor: BRAP scope — 301 reform points, 15 areas, state rankings

statement_analysis.statement: DPIIT coordinates EoDB reforms with over 16 central ministries and departments, and also assesses Indian states through the Business Reform Action Plan (BRAP).
statement_analysis.reason: DPIIT's dual role — federal reform coordination and state-level BRAP ranking — is accurately described here.

statement_analysis.reason: BRAP's 301 reform points across 15 areas versus EoDB's 10 parameters is accurate — BRAP is explicitly more granular and India-specific.

statement_analysis.statement: BRAP rankings are a sub-component of the World Bank's global Doing Business Index, as the Bank uses state-level BRAP scores to compute India's overall national rank.
statement_analysis.reason: BRAP is an entirely independent DPIIT initiative for state-level assessment. The World Bank's global EoDB only surveyed Mumbai and Delhi and had no linkage to BRAP scores in computing India's national rank.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students may assume that since BRAP was developed in the context of EoDB improvements, the World Bank must have formally integrated BRAP data into India's global rank computation.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: DPIIT coordinates with 16+ ministries and runs BRAP — accurate, so Statement 1 IS correct (not the answer).
Statement 2: 301 reform points, 15 areas, more granular than EoDB's 10 parameters — accurate, so Statement 2 IS correct (not the answer).
Statement 3: BRAP is NOT a World Bank sub-component — World Bank used only Mumbai and Delhi data, independent of BRAP. Statement 3 is NOT correct.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the intuitive but incorrect assumption that India's BRAP state rankings must feed into the World Bank's global computation. The reality is that the World Bank's EoDB had a fixed methodology (Mumbai and Delhi survey) entirely independent of any DPIIT ranking framework. BRAP was developed as a domestic policy tool — not a World Bank data input.
solution.final_explanation:
DPIIT's role in India's EoDB ecosystem operates at two distinct levels — national coordination and state-level assessment.

• Statement 1 — Correct: DPIIT's role as nodal agency for EoDB is well-established — it coordinated reform implementation across 16+ ministries and tracked progress against EoDB parameters.
• Statement 2 — Correct: BRAP's 301 reform points across 15 areas is accurate and is a key contrast point with EoDB's 10-parameter framework — BRAP is far more granular and captures India-specific regulatory realities.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (NOT correct): BRAP is an independent DPIIT framework — it was not used by the World Bank as an input for computing India's global EoDB rank. The World Bank's methodology was fixed: survey two cities (Mumbai and Delhi), use standardized case-study firms, and compute ranks based on 10 parameters. BRAP data had no formal role in this computation.

Value Addition:
• BRAP covers areas like single window systems, inspection reforms, contract enforcement, and e-governance — beyond the 10 EoDB parameters.
• States self-report reforms under BRAP, which are then verified — a different methodology from World Bank's expert-interview approach.

Step 2 — Is R correct? Equal weighting across all 10 parameters is a confirmed EoDB methodology feature — R is correct.

solution.final_explanation:
This assertion-reason probes understanding of EoDB's equal-weighting mechanism and its implication for single-parameter reforms.

Assertion (A): GST reforms improved India's Paying Taxes score, but because other parameters like Enforcing Contracts remained very poorly ranked, the composite rank improvement was limited. This is correct — India's Paying Taxes rank (~115 in DB2020) improved modestly, but Enforcing Contracts (rank 163) and Trading Across Borders held back the composite.

Reason (R): The EoDB assigned equal weight to all 10 parameters in computing the composite DTF score and overall rank. This is correct — no parameter received higher or lower weight.

Causal Link: R directly and correctly explains A. Because all 10 parameters are equally weighted, improving Paying Taxes from, say, rank 130 to rank 115 provides only 1/10th of the composite score benefit. Simultaneously, a rank of 163 in Enforcing Contracts exerts equal negative weight. R is the precise causal explanation for why single-parameter improvements have bounded composite rank effects.

Value Addition:
• This equal-weighting design meant India had to reform across all 10 parameters simultaneously to see large composite rank jumps — no single reform was sufficient.
• India's fastest rank gains came during 2016–2018 precisely because reforms were implemented across multiple parameters simultaneously.
• DTF (Distance to Frontier) measures the gap from the best global practice — improvement in DTF score is the actual metric, with rank derived from relative DTF standings.

solution.concept_anchor: EoDB measures de jure regulations not de facto implementation
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because the scenario describes bureaucratic delays and corruption — students who know EoDB tries to capture business environment may assume it measures these real-world factors too.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a gap between what the law says (procedures reformed, timelines mandated) and what actually happens (delays, unofficial payments persist).
This is the classic 'de jure vs de facto' limitation of EoDB.
Eliminate (a): EoDB can partially capture de jure improvements — it does measure procedure count and mandated timelines. But it cannot capture corruption or unofficial payments.
Eliminate (b): The scenario is not about coverage of cities — the limitation described is about what type of information is collected (legal norms vs. ground reality).
Eliminate (d): Equal weighting explains composite rank mechanics, not the de jure/de facto gap.
Confirm (c): The core limitation — EoDB measured written laws and procedures, not actual implementation — directly matches the scenario's description of the gap.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is designed to trap students who know EoDB has limitations and immediately reach for 'it can't measure everything' without specifying the precise limitation — the de jure/de facto gap. Option (a) says EoDB 'can capture' real-world impediments through its case-study methodology, which is the opposite of the truth. The case-study methodology actually reinforces the de jure limitation by relying on expert responses about written procedures.
solution.final_explanation:
The scenario describes the fundamental de jure vs. de facto gap in the EoDB methodology.

The company's experience illustrates that legal reforms on paper (shorter mandated timelines, fewer procedures) did not translate into on-the-ground improvement — delays persisted, unofficial payments were expected. This is precisely what the EoDB could not capture.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: EoDB cannot capture real-world impediments like informal payments or inspector discretion. Its case-study methodology asks experts 'what does the law require?' — not 'what actually happens?' The claim that EoDB 'can capture' such factors is incorrect.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The two-city limitation (Mumbai/Delhi) is a real criticism but is about geographic representation, not the de jure/de facto gap described in the scenario.
• Option (c) — Correct: EoDB measured 'de jure' regulations — the written law, the mandated procedures, the official timelines. It could not and did not capture de facto implementation, corruption, or informal costs. This is the scenario's core illustration.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Equal weighting is a methodological feature affecting rank computation, not the gap between legal text and implementation reality.

Value Addition:
• The de jure/de facto gap is the single most cited academic criticism of the EoDB index.
• B-READY attempts to partially address this by assessing actual public service delivery rather than only regulatory text.
• World Governance Indicators (World Bank) measure perceived corruption and rule of law — dimensions EoDB explicitly excluded.

statement_analysis.statement: India's FDI inflows increased alongside its Doing Business rank improvement between 2014 and 2020, demonstrating that higher EoDB rank directly causes higher FDI inflows.

statement_analysis.reason: This accurately states the documented FDI figure for FY2020-21 and correctly notes that India's EoDB rank had stagnated at 63 — demonstrating the limits of rank-investment correlation.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know Statement 1 is wrong (reversed causation) may overlook Statement 2 as also incorrect, assuming 'DPIIT and RBI both count FDI, so they use the same numbers.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 'directly causes' is the flaw — correlation ≠ causation. FDI was also driven by PLI, market size, global supply chain realignment. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2: DPIIT and RBI use different methodologies — DPIIT is broader (equity + reinvested earnings + other capital), RBI uses BoP methodology. 'Identical' is false. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Statement 3: FDI of $81.97 billion in FY2020-21 despite rank stagnation at 63 — accurately stated, so Statement 3 IS correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses 'reversed-causation' — presenting a correlation (FDI and rank both improved 2014–2020) as direct causation. This is a classic econometric fallacy that UPSC exploits. Students who associate 'rank improvement → better investment environment → more FDI' in a linear mental model will accept Statement 1 without questioning causality. Statement 2's trap is the assumption that two government bodies counting the same thing must use the same methodology.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between EoDB rank and FDI inflows is correlational, not causal — a distinction UPSC frequently tests.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (NOT correct): While India's FDI inflows did increase alongside rank improvement (2014–2020), this is a correlation, not causation. PLI schemes across 14 sectors, India's large domestic market, and global supply chain diversification (China+1 strategy) were independent, powerful drivers of FDI that operated simultaneously with rank improvement.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (NOT correct): DPIIT and RBI count FDI using different methodologies. DPIIT's definition is broader (equity inflows + reinvested earnings + other capital); RBI follows IMF's Balance of Payments Manual methodology. The figures from the two institutions differ and are not directly comparable.
• Statement 3 — Correct: India received ~$81.97 billion FDI in FY2020-21 — a then-record — despite the EoDB rank plateauing at 63, demonstrating that index rank is neither necessary nor sufficient for high FDI.

Value Addition:
• PLI (Production Linked Incentive) schemes were introduced across 14 sectors including pharmaceuticals, electronics, textiles, and automobiles — major FDI attractors independent of EoDB rank.
• FDI Policy circulars are issued by DPIIT; actual FDI data is captured by RBI in its balance-of-payments statistics.
• China+1 strategy — companies diversifying manufacturing out of China — was a key structural driver of India's FDI surge in 2020-21.
